Diane. Operations, Chicago. Please tell me your morning is worse than mine, because mine started at five.
Six, but with two children to get to school first. My commute is four minutes, though, so I am not going to complain.
Four minutes. I hate you a little bit. So what does the rest of it look like?
I tend to be at the office by half past eight, and the morning is back-to-back until lunch. On a bad day I put out fires until three and get to the real work after everybody has gone home.
That was my entire life until about two years ago. What changed for you?
Honestly, not enough yet. I used to be on site every day, and I do miss it. I am used to the office now, but I would not say I chose it.
Here is the only thing that worked for me. I block out two hours on Wednesday afternoon and I defend them like a client meeting. Everybody thinks it is free time.
And nobody argues with a client meeting. I might steal that. What happens in those two hours — is it thinking, or is it the work you never fit in?

The first hour is the only hour that belongs to me, so I block it out, before anybody arrives. If I do not block it out, the day takes it. That is not a productivity trick, it is just arithmetic. By ten o'clock, on a normal day, something has gone wrong on one of the sites, and once you are running behind at ten you are running behind at six. So the morning becomes putting out fires instead of the work I actually planned, and I have stopped pretending that is unusual. The strange part is what I miss. I used to be on site every day, when I was still an engineer, and there was a version of me that thought the office would be a promotion. I am used to it now. I am not going to say I like it. Ask anybody who came up through the field: we all miss the noise.

I can tell by eight o'clock what kind of day it is going to be, and the sign is very simple. Two calls before eight. One call before eight is normal, that is just somebody who wants to catch me early. Two calls before eight means somebody has been awake with the problem since six and has finally decided to share it. And here is the thing about a day that is back-to-back from nine: it has no room in it. None. So the first thing that goes wrong at half past nine pushes everything behind it, and by four in the afternoon I am apologizing to people I have never kept waiting before. The rule I made for myself, after about ten years of this, is that I keep one window in the afternoon completely empty, on purpose. Everybody who looks at my calendar thinks it is free time. It is the only reason the week does not fall over.

A study published this month looked inside the calendars of just over four hundred senior executives, and the headline figure is one that most of them would probably recognize: roughly seventy per cent of the working week was spent in meetings, and the great majority of those meetings had been booked by somebody else. What the researchers did not expect was the second finding. The executives who described themselves as being in control of their own time did not have fewer meetings. They had almost exactly the same number. What they had was two hours, in the same place in the week, blocked out for years and defended the way other people defend a client. And a note on the language, because it matters. We call that part of the week downtime, which makes it sound as though nothing is happening. On the evidence here, it is the only part of the week where anything actually gets decided.
